title: Vayishlach: Esau's family (Genesis 35:29–36:43)
hookLine: the brothers bury Isaac together, and Esau's descendants are listed with care

lines: THE OTHER SIDE OF THE FAMILY.
cards: At a family reunion, there's always the other side. The cousins from your uncle's marriage, the ones you see once every five years. Different town, different jokes, different photos on the fridge.
You're polite. You don't really know their story. Genesis 36 is that other side of the family: a long list of names, easy to let your eyes slide right over.
But it comes right after a funeral, and it's there on purpose.

teach.b: First, the funeral. Isaac dies at a hundred and eighty, old and full of days, and the text says his sons Esau and Jacob buried him. When Abraham died, Isaac was named before Ishmael.
Here the older brother, Esau, comes first. The two brothers who fought in the womb, and over a blessing, stand together at their father's grave. Then the Torah turns, not to Jacob, but to Esau.

These are the generations of Esau, who is Edom: his wives, his sons, his grandsons. Esau moved his whole household to the hill country of Seir, because the land couldn't hold both brothers' flocks. No war, no curse.

Then come chiefs, and a list of the kings who reigned in Edom before any king reigned over Israel. Esau's family had kings first, and the Torah says so, calmly. One name in the list caught the rabbis' eye: Timna.
The Talmud tells a story about her. She wanted to join Abraham's family and was turned away, so she became the concubine of Esau's son instead, and from her descended Amalek, later Israel's enemy.
The rabbis' lesson: be careful whom you push away.
Later the Torah says it plainly, in the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite, for he is thy brother."
God gave Esau his land too, Deuteronomy says, and Israel was told not to fight over it. A whole chapter for the brother who wasn't chosen, every name written down with care.

how: The genealogy of Esau is read aloud in synagogues each year as part of Vayishlach, every name included, and Jewish teachers point to Deuteronomy's command not to abhor an Edomite.

games.q: you're writing the family history. Isaac has died, and the story will follow Jacob. what do you do with Esau?
o: give his family a whole chapter.
games.why: the Torah gives Esau's family all of Genesis 36, and later says: do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother.

practice: Picture a family you tend to overlook: your in-laws, the neighbors with different customs, the side of the family you don't call.
Imagine their list of names, grandparents, children, the people they've buried, the ones they're proud of. Let their story become as real as yours for a minute.

orig.note: Hebrew: Edom, red. Esau's other name, and the name of his people.

carryVoice: Your line: his story matters too. Brothers who fought stood together at the grave. Two hundred days, and counting.
